title: Krishna Points Out Karna's Rampage and Urges Arjuna
one_line_summary: Krishna, as Arjuna's charioteer, shows Arjuna how Yudhishthira is being pursued and how Karna is ravaging the Pandava army, urging him to advance and slay Karna.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Meanwhile Krishna, pointing out king Yudhishthira the just, unto Kunti's son Partha, addressed him in these words: 'Yonder, O son of Pandu, your brother (Yudhishthira) is being pursued by many mighty and great bowmen... Righteously setting thy heart on battle, advance against that leader of car-warriors.'
notes: Krishna as charioteer narrates the live battle to Arjuna; chiefly Krishna's counsel rather than combat.

title: Krishna Advises Arjuna to See the Wounded King First
one_line_summary: Krishna tells Arjuna that Yudhishthira has been deeply wounded by Karna and advises him to first see and comfort the king before slaying Karna.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Thus addressed by Partha, Krishna replied unto that foremost of intelligent men... 'The royal son of Kunti hath been deeply wounded and mangled by Karna. Having seen him first and comforted him, thou wilt then, O Partha, slay Karna.'
notes: Krishna deliberately times the confrontation so Karna will be fatigued.

title: Krishna Drives Arjuna to Yudhishthira's Side
one_line_summary: Krishna drives the chariot at great speed to the wounded Yudhishthira, and the two Krishnas alight and worship the king's feet.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Then Hrishikesha proceeded with very great speed to the spot where king Yudhishthira was... Then those two foremost of men, (Krishna and Arjuna), proceeding on their car, approached the king who was lying alone on his bed. Both of them, alighting from that car, worshipped the feet of king Yudhishthira the just.

title: Krishna Offers Sudarsana to Slay Karna
one_line_summary: Seeing Karna baffle Arjuna's weapons, Krishna rebukes Arjuna's slackness and offers him the razor-edged Sudarsana discus to strike off Karna's head.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Then Vasudeva, beholding Partha's shafts baffled by Karna, said unto the former, 'What is this, O diadem-decked Arjuna, that Karna should succeed in crushing thy weapons today... Putting forth thy might, strike off the head of that foe of thine with this Sudarsana, of edge keen as a razor, that I give unto thee, like Sakra striking off the head of his foe Namuci, with the thunderbolt.'
notes: The rare moment Krishna offers his own discus Sudarsana to a mortal.

title: Krishna Sinks the Chariot to Save Arjuna
one_line_summary: When Karna looses the snake-arrow Aswasena at Arjuna's head, Krishna presses the chariot down into the earth with his feet so that the arrow only sweeps off Arjuna's diadem.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Beholding that shaft blazing in the welkin, the slayer of Kamsa, Madhava, with great speed and the greatest ease, pressed down with his feet that excellent car, causing it to sink about a cubit deep. At this, the steeds, white as the rays of the moon... bending their knees, laid themselves down on the ground.
notes: Krishna's quick action turns a fatal head-shot into the loss of Arjuna's diadem.

title: Krishna Identifies the Snake Aswasena
one_line_summary: Krishna names the attacking snake as Aswasena, whose mother Arjuna slew at Khandava, bids Arjuna slay it, and after Arjuna cuts it down raises the sunken chariot with his arms.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Krishna replied, 'Whilst thou, armed with bow, wert engaged at Khandava in gratifying the god Agni, this snake was then in the sky, his body ensconced within his mother's... Remembering that act of hostility done by thee, he cometh towards thee today for thy destruction.' ... After that snake had been cut off by Arjuna, the lord Keshava himself... raised up with his arms that car from the earth.

title: Krishna Urges Arjuna to Slay the Distressed Karna
one_line_summary: When Arjuna hesitates to strike the stupefied Karna, Krishna urges him not to spare a fallen foe; Karna's chariot-wheel then sinks into the earth and he appeals to Arjuna's righteousness for a moment's respite.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: The younger brother of Indra then, with great excitement, addressed him, saying, 'Why, O son of Pandu, dost thou become so forgetful? They that are truly wise never spare their foes, however weak, even for a moment... Slay him, therefore, like Indra slaying the Asura Namuci.'
notes: Karna's death itself falls in section 91 (outside this bundle); section 90 ends with Karna's wheel stuck and his appeal for mercy.

title: Krishna Substitutes an Iron Statue for Bhima
one_line_summary: Sensing Dhritarashtra's murderous intent, Krishna drags away the real Bhima and substitutes an iron statue, which the blind king crushes in his embrace; Krishna then reveals the trick and consoles him.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Ascertaining the evil intentions cherished by him towards Bhima, Krishna, dragging away the real Bhima, presented an iron statue of the second son of Pandu to the old king... Understanding that he was no longer under the influence of wrath... Vasudeva, that foremost of men, said these words, 'Do not grieve, O Dhritarashtra, for thou hast not slain Bhimasena! That is an iron statue, O king, which has been broken by thee!'
notes: The 'embrace-that-fails' episode; in this edition it is in Stri-parva section 12, not 25 as the task description suggested.

title: Krishna Counsels Dhritarashtra to Govern His Wrath
one_line_summary: Krishna admonishes Dhritarashtra that his sorrow is his own fault and urges him to restrain his wrath; the king is pacified and embraces and blesses the Pandavas.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: 'Why then dost thou cherish such wrath when all that has overtaken thee is the result of thy own fault? ... Recollecting thy own faults, govern thy wrath now.' ... 'Now, however, I am free from wrath and fever. I desire eagerly, O Madhava, to embrace that hero, the second son of Pandu.'

title: Gandhari Curses Krishna; He Accepts with a Smile
one_line_summary: Grieving her sons, Gandhari curses Krishna that in the thirty-sixth year he will see his own kinsmen slain and himself perish in the wilderness; Krishna, smiling, accepts that only the Vrishnis themselves can destroy the Vrishnis.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Since thou wert indifferent to the Kurus and the Pandavas whilst they slew each other, therefore, O Govinda, thou shalt be the slayer of thy own kinsmen! In the thirty-sixth year from this... thou shalt... perish by disgusting means in the wilderness. Hearing these words, the high-souled Vasudeva... said unto her these words, with a faint smile, 'There is none in the world, save myself, that is capable of exterminating the Vrishnis... In uttering this curse, O thou of excellent vows, thou hast aided me in the accomplishment of that task.'
notes: Gandhari's curse is in section 25, not 15 as the task description stated.

title: Krishna Rebukes Gandhari
one_line_summary: Krishna tells Gandhari to arise and not grieve, declaring the carnage came through her own fault and Duryodhana's wickedness, not through him.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: 'Arise, arise, O Gandhari, do not set thy heart on grief! Through thy fault, this vast carnage has taken place! Thy son Duryodhana was wicked-souled, envious, and exceedingly arrogant... Why dost thou wish to ascribe thy own faults to me?'

title: Arjuna Asks Krishna to Repeat the Gita; Krishna Offers the Anugita
one_line_summary: After the war, Arjuna confesses he has forgotten the Gita's teaching and asks Krishna to repeat it; Krishna says he cannot recite it again in detail and instead narrates an old history (the Anugita).

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Arjuna... addressed his companion, saying, '...What thy holy self said unto me at that time, O Kesava, through affection, has all been forgotten by me, O chief of men, in consequence of the fickleness of my mind.' ... Vasudeva said, '...It is impossible for me, O Dhananjaya, to repeat, in detail, all that I said on that occasion... I shalt now, however, recite to thee an old history upon the same topic.'
notes: Frame of the Anugita; sections 17-20 are the Brahmana's discourse (pure teaching, no narrative events extracted).

title: The Sages Curse the Vrishnis Through Samva
one_line_summary: The Vrishni youths disguise Samva as a pregnant woman to mock the sages, who curse that Samva will bring forth an iron bolt to destroy the Vrishnis and Andhakas, with Rama entering the ocean and Jara slaying Krishna; Krishna, informed, accepts the destiny.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: 'This heir of Vasudeva, by name Samva, will bring forth a fierce iron bolt for the destruction of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas... The blessed hero armed with the plough will enter the ocean, casting off his body, while a hunter of the name of Jara will pierce the high-souled Krishna while lying on the ground.' ... The slayer of Madhu, informed of what had taken place, summoned all the Vrishnis and told them of it... he simply said that that which was destined would surely happen.

title: Samva Brings Forth the Iron Bolt; Wine Is Prohibited
one_line_summary: The next day Samva brings forth the iron bolt; king Ugrasena has it ground to powder and cast into the sea, and at the command of Krishna, Rama and others a prohibition on wine is proclaimed throughout Dwaraka.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: When the next day came, Samva actually brought forth an iron bolt through which all the individuals in the race of the Vrishnis and the Andhakas became consumed into ashes... In great distress of mind, the king (Ugrasena) caused that iron bolt to be reduced into fine powder... it was, again, proclaimed throughout the city that from that day, among all the Vrishnis and the Andhakas no one should manufacture wines and intoxicating spirits of any kind.

title: Krishna Commands a Pilgrimage to Prabhasa
one_line_summary: Seeing the evil omens and the inauspicious lunation, Krishna, understanding that Gandhari's curse is being fulfilled, commands the Vrishnis to make a pilgrimage to the sea-coast to bathe in the ocean.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Hrishikesa, summoning the Yadavas, said unto them these words: 'The fourteenth lunation has been made the fifteenth by Rahu once more... It has once more appeared, it seems, for our destruction.' ... Vasudeva, having said so, endeavoured to bring about those occurrences which would make Gandhari's words true. That chastiser of foes commanded the Vrishnis to make a pilgrimage to some sacred water.
notes: Krishna actively moves events toward the fulfilment of Gandhari's curse.

title: Uddhava Departs; Krishna Does Not Prevent Him
one_line_summary: As the Yadavas encamp at Prabhasa, Uddhava comes to take his leave; Krishna salutes him and, knowing the destruction of the Vrishnis is at hand, does not prevent his departure.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Hearing that they had taken up their abode on the sea-coast, Uddhava, the wisest of men, who was, besides, well-versed in Yoga, proceeded there and took his leave (for departing). Krishna, with joined hands, saluted Uddhava, and seeing him bent on departing (from the world) and knowing that the destructions of the Vrishnis was at hand, did not feel any disposition to prevent him.

title: The Drunken Quarrel at Prabhasa
one_line_summary: At the Prabhasa revels, the drunken Satyaki taunts Kritavarma about the night-slaughter, Kritavarma retorts, and in the ensuing fury Satyaki beheads Kritavarma in Krishna's sight, igniting the general brawl.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Then Yuyudhana, inebriated with wine, derisively laughing at and insulting Kritavarma in the midst of that assembly, said, 'What Kshatriya is there who... will slay men locked in the embraces of sleep and, therefore, already dead?' ... Having said these words, Satyaki rushed at Kritavarma and severed his head with a sword in the very sight of Keshava.

title: Krishna's Eraka Grass Becomes an Iron Bolt
one_line_summary: Seeing his son Pradyumna and Satyaki slain, Krishna takes up a handful of Eraka grass that becomes an iron thunderbolt, and the Yadavas destroy one another — son killing sire — until Krishna exterminates the Vrishnis and Andhakas.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: The delighter of the Yadus, beholding his own son, and the son of Sini too, slain, took up, in wrath, a handful of the Eraka grass that grew there. That handful of grass became a terrible bolt of iron endued with the energy of the thunderbolt. With it Krishna slew all those that came before him... Son killed sire, and sire killed son, O Bharata.
notes: The mutual slaughter at Prabhasa fulfils the Brahmanas' curse.

title: Krishna Sends Daruka for Arjuna; Vabhru Is Slain
one_line_summary: Krishna sends Daruka to summon Arjuna and commands Vabhru to protect the women; Vabhru, still dazed with wine, is slain by the iron bolt that springs from a hunter's mallet.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Krishna commanded Daruka, saying, 'Going to the Kurus, inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus. Let Arjuna come here quickly...' ... Vabhru... as soon as he had proceeded to a distance, the iron-bolt, attaching itself to a mallet in the hands of a hunter, suddenly sprang of itself upon that solitary survivor of the Yadava race and slew him.

title: Krishna Entrusts the Women to Vasudeva
one_line_summary: Krishna returns to Dwaraka, tells his father Vasudeva to protect the women until Arjuna comes, touches his father's feet, and retraces his steps to comfort the wailing ladies.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Entering the city of Dwaravati, Janardana said these words unto his father, 'Do thou protect all the ladies of our house, till Dhananjaya comes...' Having said these words, Krishna touched the feet of his father with his head, and quickly left his presence. Then a loud wail of sorrow arose from the ladies... Keshava retraced his foot-steps and said unto them, 'Arjuna will come here. That foremost of men will relieve you of your grief.'

title: Balarama Departs as the White Serpent
one_line_summary: Krishna finds Balarama seated in Yoga in the forest; a great white thousand-headed serpent (Sesha) issues from his mouth and, welcomed by the ocean and celestial serpents, Balarama departs the world.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Proceeding then to the forest, Keshava beheld Rama sitting in a solitary spot thereof. He also saw that Rama had set himself to Yoga and that from out his mouth was issuing a mighty snake. The colour of that snake was white... that high-souled naga of a 1,000 heads... proceeded along that way which led to the ocean.

title: The Hunter Jara Pierces Krishna's Heel
one_line_summary: Krishna sits in deep Yoga, recollecting Gandhari's curse and Durvasas's words; the hunter Jara, mistaking his foot for a deer, pierces Krishna's heel with an arrow.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Having restrained all his senses, speech, and mind, Krishna laid himself down in high Yoga. A fierce hunter of the name of Jara then came there, desirous of deer. The hunter, mistaking Keshava, who was stretched on the earth in high Yoga, for a deer, pierced him at the heel with a shaft and quickly came to that spot for capturing his prey.

title: Krishna Comforts Jara and Ascends to Heaven
one_line_summary: Jara, seeing the four-armed Krishna, falls at his feet in fear; Krishna comforts him, then ascends filling the welkin with splendour, and the gods receive him in Heaven.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: Coming up, Jara beheld a man dressed in yellow robes, rapt in Yoga and endued with many arms. Regarding himself an offender, and filled with fear, he touched the feet of Keshava. The high-souled one comforted him and then ascended upwards, filling the entire welkin with splendour. When he reached Heaven, Vasava and the twin Ashvinis and Rudra and the Adityas... advanced to receive him.

title: Dwaraka Is Swallowed by the Ocean
one_line_summary: As Arjuna leads the surviving Vrishni women and children away, the ocean floods and swallows the abandoned city of Dwaraka, fulfilling Krishna's own prophecy.

primary_source.work: Mahabharata (Kisari Mohan Ganguli English translation, all 18 parvas)

source_excerpt: After all the people had set out, the ocean, that home of sharks and alligators, flooded Dwaraka, which still teemed with wealth of every kind, with its waters. Whatever portion of the ground was passed over, ocean immediately flooded over with his waters. Beholding this wonderful sight, the inhabitants of Dwaraka walked faster and faster, saying, 'Wonderful is the course of fate!'
notes: Fulfils Krishna's parting words to Vasudeva that the sea would swallow Dwaravati after Arjuna's departure.
